Reference: Tsivanidis (2026)

Model Setting

The paper asks how large the economic gains from urban public transit are once people can change where they live and work, firms can relocate, and wages and floorspace prices adjust. The setting is TransMilenio in Bogota, the world's most-used bus rapid transit (BRT) system: opened in 2000 and extended in 2006 and 2012, it has 147 stations and more than 2.2 million daily riders, with dedicated lanes, operating speeds of about 26 km per hour (against roughly 10 km per hour on the incumbent buses), and feeder buses to terminals at no extra fare. Before the system, 73 percent of commuters used buses, car commutes were about 36 percent faster than bus commutes, and low-educated residents were about 23 percent more likely to use buses, so the distributional effects are also of interest. The standard evaluation tool is the value of travel time savings (VTTS), which misses reallocation and general equilibrium effects.

The paper builds a quantitative urban model with two skill groups, car ownership, several commute modes, nonhomothetic (Stone-Geary) housing demand, multiple industries, and productivity and amenity externalities. A special case with one group yields a log-linear reduced form in which the transit network matters only through commuter market access (CMA): resident CMA (access to jobs) and firm CMA (access to workers). The elasticities of population, employment and floorspace prices to CMA, together with the change in CMA, are sufficient statistics for the effects of transit in a broad class of models. These elasticities are estimated on 2,799 census tracts with data from before and after construction. The main findings are that the VTTS captures only 52 percent of the general equilibrium welfare gain (1.25 against 2.39 percent); that welfare rose by 2.34 percent and GDP by 3.25 percent in a closed city (0.69 and 17.5 percent with migration); that the high-skilled gain slightly more, so welfare inequality rises by a modest 0.59 percent; and that a well-targeted zoning reform would have raised the welfare gain by about 36 percent.

Equilibrium

Given location characteristics {Hi,uˉiag,Aˉjs,tija,τi}\{H_i,\bar{u}_{iag},\bar{A}_{js},t_{ija},\tau_i\}{Hi​,uˉiag​,Aˉjs​,tija​,τi​}, populations {Lˉg}\{\bar{L}_g\}{Lˉg​} and parameters, an equilibrium is a vector {LRiag,LFjg,wjg,rRi,rFi,ϑi,Uˉg,π}\{L_{Riag},L_{Fjg},w_{jg},r_{Ri},r_{Fi},\vartheta_i,\bar{U}_g,\pi\}{LRiag​,LFjg​,wjg​,rRi​,rFi​,ϑi​,Uˉg​,π} such that (i) labor supply to each workplace equals firms' labor demand; (ii) residential and commercial floorspace markets clear, with residential prices consistent with the residential supply equation and floorspace shares consistent with landowner optimality; and (iii) the city is closed and land rents are rebated lump sum to residents:

Lˉg=∑i,aLRiag∀g,π=Lˉ−1∑i(rRiHRi+rFiHFi)(17)\bar{L}_g=\sum_{i,a}L_{Riag}\quad\forall g,\qquad\pi=\bar{L}^{-1}\sum_i\left(r_{Ri}H_{Ri}+r_{Fi}H_{Fi}\right) \tag{17}Lˉg​=i,a∑​LRiag​∀g,π=Lˉ−1i∑​(rRi​HRi​+rFi​HFi​)(17)

where Lˉ\bar{L}Lˉ is total population. Rebating rents to residents keeps all gains inside the model and avoids the inefficiency of absentee landlords, which matters for the welfare result below. With externalities there may be multiple equilibria; counterfactuals start the solution algorithm from the observed equilibrium.

Commuter Market Access and the Reduced Form

Consider the special case with one group of workers and firms, no fixed elements of expenditure or income (hˉ=pcar=0\bar{h}=p_{car}=0hˉ=pcar​=0), and fixed floorspace supplies. Substituting the labor supply relation wjθ=LFj/ΦFjw_j^{\theta}=L_{Fj}/\Phi_{Fj}wjθ​=LFj​/ΦFj​ into the definitions of the two access terms shows that they solve:

ΦRi=∑jdij−θLFjΦFj,ΦFj=∑idij−θLRiΦRi(18)\Phi_{Ri}=\sum_jd_{ij}^{-\theta}\frac{L_{Fj}}{\Phi_{Fj}},\qquad\Phi_{Fj}=\sum_id_{ij}^{-\theta}\frac{L_{Ri}}{\Phi_{Ri}} \tag{18}ΦRi​=j∑​dij−θ​ΦFj​LFj​​,ΦFj​=i∑​dij−θ​ΦRi​LRi​​(18)

so CMA can be recovered (uniquely up to scale) from residential populations LRiL_{Ri}LRi​, employment LFjL_{Fj}LFj​, commute costs dij=exp⁡(κtij)d_{ij}=\exp(\kappa t_{ij})dij​=exp(κtij​) and the commuting elasticity θ\thetaθ alone, without wage data. RCMA is high where a location is close to employment, especially employment in places that themselves lack access to workers (and so pay high wages); FCMA is high where a location is close to residents, especially residents who lack access to jobs. Unlike market access in trade models with balanced trade, the two differ because residence and employment do not coincide: TransMilenio raised RCMA most in the outskirts and FCMA most in the center.

(3) Level changes, including the change in welfare Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ and in city population, also require an assumption on migration between the city and the rest of the country and values for σD\sigma_DσD​ and β\betaβ. (4) Parts 1 and 2 hold in any model with a gravity equation for commuting whose equilibrium can be written as KKK equations in KKK endogenous variables y1i,…,yKiy_{1i},\ldots,y_{Ki}y1i​,…,yKi​ of the form:

∏k=1Kykiαkh=λhΦRibhRΦFibhFeihfor h=1,…,K(21)\prod_{k=1}^{K}y_{ki}^{\alpha_{kh}}=\lambda_h\Phi_{Ri}^{b^R_h}\Phi_{Fi}^{b^F_h}e_{ih}\qquad\text{for }h=1,\ldots,K \tag{21}k=1∏K​ykiαkh​​=λh​ΦRibhR​​ΦFibhF​​eih​for h=1,…,K(21)

This class includes isoelastic housing supply, endogenous firm location, capital in production, Eaton and Kortum (2002) production, leisure, preference instead of productivity shocks, and alternative timing assumptions. The intuition is that the network enters every equilibrium condition only through ΦRi\Phi_{Ri}ΦRi​ and ΦFi\Phi_{Fi}ΦFi​, so inverting a log-linear system gives each outcome as a log-linear function of the two access terms. Models in the class differ in how structural parameters map into βR\boldsymbol{\beta}_RβR​ and βF\boldsymbol{\beta}_FβF​, but given these elasticities they deliver identical relative counterfactuals, so the researcher need not take a stand on which model is true. Only the level of the effects depends on the particular structural parameters {αkh,bhR,bhF}\{\alpha_{kh},b^R_h,b^F_h\}{αkh​,bhR​,bhF​}.

Welfare and the Value of Travel Time Savings

Proposition 2 (first-order welfare effect). When the equilibrium is efficient, applying the envelope theorem to the planner's problem shows that the elasticity of welfare to a change in transit infrastructure is proportional to a weighted average of the time savings on each commute. This is exactly the VTTS formula used in transport appraisal (Train and McFadden 1978; Small and Verhoef 2007): to first order, reallocation of residents, jobs and floorspace has no welfare effect of its own, and the changes in wages and floorspace prices are transfers. The general equilibrium gain can therefore differ from the VTTS for only two reasons: the shock is large, so the first-order approximation is poor (commuters re-optimize toward the improved links), or the equilibrium is inefficient because of the productivity and amenity externalities μA\mu_AμA​ and μU\mu_UμU​. The exact expression is in the supplemental appendix and is not reproduced here.

Data and Measuring CMA

The unit of analysis is the census tract (2,799 tracts, mean population 2,429 in 2005). Residential population by education comes from the 1993, 2005 and 2018 censuses; employment from the 1990 economic census, the 2005 census and chamber of commerce establishment registries for 2000 and 2015; floorspace prices and uses for 2000 to 2018 from the city cadastre, which covers 98.6 percent of properties; commuting from the 1995, 2005, 2011 and 2015 Mobility Surveys; and wages from household surveys. Commute times by mode between tracts are computed on the digitized networks.

The mode choice parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood on 2015 trip data (19,510 trips): κ=0.012\kappa=0.012κ=0.012, λ=0.138\lambda=0.138λ=0.138, bBus=−0.085b_{Bus}=-0.085bBus​=−0.085, bCar=0.853b_{Car}=0.853bCar​=0.853 and bTM=−0.212b_{TM}=-0.212bTM​=−0.212, so cars are most attractive conditional on time and TransMilenio least (crowding, walking to stations). Average times tijt_{ij}tij​ weight tij0t_{ij0}tij0​ and tij1t_{ij1}tij1​ by the city-wide share of car owners. The special case implies a gravity equation in changes, estimated by PPML on locality pairs for 1995 and 2015 with origin-destination, origin-year and destination-year fixed effects; it gives θκ=0.039\theta\kappa=0.039θκ=0.039 and θ=3.401\theta=3.401θ=3.401. For the full model, differencing the commuting probability gives:

with fixed effects γiag\gamma_{iag}γiag​ and δjg\delta_{jg}δjg​ and unobserved commute costs εijag\varepsilon_{ijag}εijag​. The preferred IV estimates are θH=2.44\theta_H=2.44θH​=2.44 and θL=4\theta_L=4θL​=4: the high-skilled have more dispersed match productivities and less elastic commuting.

Reduced-Form Estimation

The two reduced-form equations are estimated in long differences across tracts. Because changes in CMA contain population and employment in both periods, which respond to the amenity and productivity shocks in the residuals, the regressor is the change in CMA obtained by solving the CMA system with population and employment held at their initial levels, changing only commute costs, and excluding the tract itself from the sums. Route placement may still be endogenous, and the paper combines several strategies: (i) locality fixed effects, distance to the center by region, and tract, historical and land market controls; (ii) using only changes in the network more than 1.5 km away; (iii) controlling for proximity to stations, to separate access from other station effects; (iv) controlling for the average change in CMA under four unbuilt historical subway plans, which is both a placebo and the recentering of Borusyak and Hull (2023) for non-random exposure; (v) instruments based on a least-cost construction path and on the 1921 tram network; and (vi) the staggered opening of three phases. The falsification test for the last is:

Δt,t−ℓln⁡yi=βCurrentΔt,t−ℓln⁡Φi+βFutureΔt+k,tln⁡Φi+γ′Xi+εi(23)\Delta_{t,t-\ell}\ln y_i=\beta^{Current}\Delta_{t,t-\ell}\ln\Phi_i+\beta^{Future}\Delta_{t+k,t}\ln\Phi_i+\gamma'X_i+\varepsilon_i \tag{23}Δt,t−ℓ​lnyi​=βCurrentΔt,t−ℓ​lnΦi​+βFutureΔt+k,t​lnΦi​+γ′Xi​+εi​(23)

where βFuture\beta^{Future}βFuture loads on the change in CMA from lines that open only after ttt and should be zero, and XiX_iXi​ are the baseline controls. An event study uses annual cadastral prices around the opening of phase 3:

ln⁡rRit=αi+γℓ(i)t+∑τ=−86βτΔ12,06ln⁡ΦRi+δt′Xi+εit(24)\ln r_{Rit}=\alpha_i+\gamma_{\ell(i)t}+\sum_{\tau=-8}^{6}\beta^{\tau}\Delta_{12,06}\ln\Phi_{Ri}+\delta_t'X_i+\varepsilon_{it} \tag{24}lnrRit​=αi​+γℓ(i)t​+τ=−8∑6​βτΔ12,06​lnΦRi​+δt′​Xi​+εit​(24)

with tract effects αi\alpha_iαi​, locality-year effects γℓ(i)t\gamma_{\ell(i)t}γℓ(i)t​ and coefficients βτ\beta^{\tau}βτ for each year τ\tauτ relative to opening.

  • Baseline elasticities (full controls, Conley standard errors): with respect to RCMA, 0.410 (0.159) for residential floorspace prices and 0.732 (0.318) for residential population; with respect to FCMA, 0.728 (0.238) for commercial floorspace prices, 0.258 (0.086) for the commercial share of floorspace and 1.508 (0.788) for establishments.

  • Robustness: estimates are stable when excluding terminals and the center, using only distant network changes, or controlling for station proximity (population 0.983, establishments 1.457). Binned scatter plots are close to log-linear, as the model predicts.

  • Placebos: the coefficients on CMA under the unbuilt plans are insignificant in all five regressions, and the coefficients on realized CMA do not move (p-values for equality between 0.16 and 0.9). Future CMA is insignificant except for total census employment (4.622, driven by outliers). Event-study coefficients are flat before opening, jump by about 0.5 in the year before opening and rise by a further 0.75 by year six.

  • IV: instrumenting realized CMA with the tram and least-cost-path measures gives similar estimates, except for a larger residential price elasticity (1.125).

Aggregate Effects from Sufficient Statistics

The counterfactual removes TransMilenio from the observed equilibrium, using the baseline elasticities with 1−α=0.2061-\alpha=0.2061−α=0.206 (floorspace share of costs), 1−β=0.2741-\beta=0.2741−β=0.274 (average housing expenditure share) and σD=6\sigma_D=6σD​=6.

  • VTTS against general equilibrium: adding the system back to the no-TransMilenio equilibrium raises welfare by 1.246 percent under the first-order (VTTS) formula and by 2.393 percent in general equilibrium (90 percent interval 0.748 to 6.360), so the VTTS captures 52 percent of the gain. Without externalities (μA=μU=0\mu_A=\mu_U=0μA​=μU​=0) the gain is 1.526 percent. Of the gap, about one quarter is due to the size of the shock and about three quarters to externalities.

  • Closed city: welfare rises by 2.337 percent, GDP by 3.247 percent (2.630 percent net of construction and operating costs) and average rents fall by 0.4 percent. This accounts for 3.1 percent of observed GDP growth from 2000 to 2016.

  • Open city (migration elasticity ρ=3\rho=3ρ=3): population rises by 11.0 percent and rents by 7.2 percent, so welfare rises by only 0.688 percent, while GDP rises by 17.5 percent (16.9 percent net of costs). This accounts for 16.6 percent of observed GDP growth and 40.3 percent of population growth.

  • Congestion: with a congestion elasticity of 0.06 (Akbar and Duranton 2017) the welfare gain is 0.56 percent larger than without congestion (4.035 against 4.013 percent in that extension). Converting the BRT lanes to car lanes would have produced 0.64 percent of the gain.

Estimating the Full Model

The αsg\alpha_{sg}αsg​ match the college wage bill share in each industry, and {hˉ,pcar,Tg}\{\bar{h},p_{car},T_g\}{hˉ,pcar​,Tg​} match the average housing expenditure share, average car expenditure and the college wage premium. The agglomeration elasticity is larger than typical developed-country estimates but imprecise, and the high-skilled value living among other high-skilled residents. Two untargeted checks support the model: a regression of observed on predicted changes in the residential floorspace share has slope 1.454 (0.722), not different from one, and the elasticity of income to RCMA is 0.522 (0.224), not different from the predicted 1/θ1/\theta1/θ.

Distributional Results

Welfare changes are computed by removing TransMilenio in the full model; inequality is Uˉ^H/Uˉ^L\hat{\bar{U}}_H/\hat{\bar{U}}_LUˉ^H​/Uˉ^L​.

  • Main result: average welfare rises by 1.197 percent (90 percent interval 0.336 to 4.198) and welfare inequality rises by 0.585 percent (interval −0.186-0.186−0.186 to 0.921). The p-value of the test that the high-skilled gain more is 0.14, so the result is suggestive.

  • Common elasticities, perfect substitutes: with the same η\etaη and θ\thetaθ for both groups, average welfare rises by 1.925 percent and inequality falls by 0.339 percent, as the low-skilled use public transit more.

  • Different commuting elasticities: allowing θH<θL\theta_H<\theta_LθH​<θL​ gives 2.140 and +0.204+0.204+0.204 percent. The high-skilled substitute less across workplaces, bear more of the incidence of slow commutes and gain more from faster ones. Adding the estimated ηg\eta_gηg​ gives 2.412 and +0.249+0.249+0.249 percent. These three averages are close to the 2.39 percent of the sufficient-statistics approach.

  • Imperfect substitutes: moving to σ=1/0.7\sigma=1/0.7σ=1/0.7 lowers the average gain to 1.197 percent, because an inflow of one skill group raises the labor composite by less, and raises the inequality effect to 0.585 percent. The high-skilled are partly shielded from the wage decline caused by the large shift in low-skilled labor supply, and the network connects the high-skilled north to skill-intensive industries in the center.

  • Extensions: with domestic services employment (7.3 percent of non-college workers) the effects are 0.999 and 0.621 percent; with local home ownership 1.045 and 0.712; with all renters 1.046 and 0.755.

Policy Counterfactuals

  • Network components: removing the southern trunk line lowers welfare by 0.409 percent and output by 0.324 percent; removing the northern line lowers welfare by 0.141 percent, inequality by 0.224 percent and output by 0.715 percent. Removing the feeder buses lowers welfare by 1.083 percent and output by 1.039 percent, more than either trunk line, which points to high returns from cheap last-mile services. Raising the operating speed to 35 km per hour would add 1.622 percent to welfare, 0.690 percent to inequality and 2.856 percent to output.

  • Housing supply: TransMilenio was not accompanied by zoning changes. If floorspace supply had responded log-linearly to prices with the elasticity of Oakland (the sixth most inelastic US city in Saiz 2010), the welfare gain would have been 35.87 percent larger and the output gain 16.50 percent larger.

  • Land value capture (LVC): the government sells development rights. Allowing up to 30 percent more floorspace within 500 m of stations raises the welfare gain by 17.82 percent and the output gain by 9.46 percent. Allocating the same number of permits according to each tract's predicted change in CMA raises them by 35.64 and 12.44 percent, almost as much as free adjustment, because permits go where demand rises most.

  • Revenue: the distance-band scheme raises 185.78 million dollars in the closed city and 493.12 million in the open city (2016 USD), or 12.82 and 34.01 percent of capital costs. The CMA-based scheme raises 281.13 and 924.77 million dollars, or 19.39 and 63.79 percent of capital costs.

The equation is the indirect utility of Stone-Geary preferences. which falls with income toward 1−β1-\beta1−β: this is the nonhomotheticity. The formula requires y>rRihˉy>r_{Ri}\bar{h}y>rRi​hˉ.

This is an assumed functional form for the commute cost of worker ω\omegaω on mode mmm between residence iii and workplace jjj. The cost is a pure number that divides labor income in equation (1): a worker who would earn wjgϵj(ω)w_{jg}\epsilon_j(\omega)wjg​ϵj​(ω) with a costless commute earns wjgϵj(ω)/dijm(ω)w_{jg}\epsilon_j(\omega)/d_{ijm}(\omega)wjg​ϵj​(ω)/dijm​(ω). Inside the exponential, tijmt_{ijm}tijm​ is travel time in minutes, κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 is the semi-elasticity of the cost to time (one more minute lowers effective income by about 100κ100\kappa100κ percent; the estimate κ=0.012\kappa=0.012κ=0.012 means 1.2 percent per minute), b~m\tilde{b}_mb~m​ is a mode preference shifter that enters with a minus sign (a higher value makes the mode less costly at given time: comfort, reliability, absence of crowding), and υijm(ω)\upsilon_{ijm}(\omega)υijm​(ω) is an idiosyncratic shock.

The exponential form makes the log cost linear, ln⁡dijm(ω)=κtijm−b~m+υijm(ω)\ln d_{ijm}(\omega)=\kappa t_{ijm}-\tilde{b}_m+\upsilon_{ijm}(\omega)lndijm​(ω)=κtijm​−b~m​+υijm​(ω), so that the choice min⁡mdijm(ω)\min_m d_{ijm}(\omega)minm​dijm​(ω) is a standard additive random utility problem; with generalized extreme value shocks it gives the nested logit and the inclusive values of equation (3). It also makes the commuting gravity equation log-linear in time with slope θgκ\theta_g\kappaθg​κ, equation (22). The form rules out monetary fares that matter differently by income and any direct dependence of the time cost on skill (the paper reports that group-specific κ\kappaκ are statistically indistinguishable).

The requirement dijm(ω)≥1d_{ijm}(\omega)\geq1dijm​(ω)≥1 stated in the note is a normalization of interpretation and is not implied by the functional form, because the shock has unbounded support.

This is the assumed productivity spillover. Productivity AjsA_{js}Ajs​ of industry sss in location jjj is the product of an exogenous fundamental Aˉjs\bar{A}_{js}Aˉjs​ (roads, slope of the land) and a power function of employment density, where L~Fj=∑sL~Fjs\tilde{L}_{Fj}=\sum_s\tilde{L}_{Fjs}L~Fj​=∑s​L~Fjs​ is total effective labor in jjj summed over industries and skill groups and TjT_jTj​ is land area. The parameter μA≥0\mu_A\geq0μA​≥0 is the elasticity of productivity to density; the GMM estimate is 0.2530.2530.253.

The spillover is external: firms take AjsA_{js}Ajs​ as given in equations (9) to (11), so no firm internalizes that hiring raises the productivity of its neighbors. This is one of the two sources of inefficiency that make the general equilibrium gain differ from the VTTS. The spillover is local (it depends only on employment in the same tract, with no spatial decay) and common across industries.

In logs, ln⁡Ajs=ln⁡Aˉjs+μAln⁡L~Fj−μAln⁡Tj\ln A_{js}=\ln\bar{A}_{js}+\mu_A\ln\tilde{L}_{Fj}-\mu_A\ln T_jlnAjs​=lnAˉjs​+μA​lnL~Fj​−μA​lnTj​. Because land area does not change over time, differencing gives the estimating equation (27), Δln⁡Ajs=μAΔln⁡L~Fj+Δln⁡Aˉjs\Delta\ln A_{js}=\mu_A\Delta\ln\tilde{L}_{Fj}+\Delta\ln\bar{A}_{js}ΔlnAjs​=μA​ΔlnL~Fj​+ΔlnAˉjs​, where the unobserved change in fundamentals is the error term and employment growth is instrumented with predicted growth in firm commuter market access. Transit raises ΦFj\Phi_{Fj}ΦFj​ in the center, employment concentrates there, and with μA>0\mu_A>0μA​>0 productivity rises: about three quarters of the gap between the general equilibrium gain and the VTTS is attributed to externalities.

This is the assumed amenity spillover. The amenity uiagu_{iag}uiag​ enjoyed by a type-ggg resident of iii with car ownership aaa is the product of an exogenous component uˉiag\bar{u}_{iag}uˉiag​ (leafy streets, proximity to getaways, which may matter differently by car ownership) and a power function of the college share of residents, LRiH/LRi∈(0,1]L_{RiH}/L_{Ri}\in(0,1]LRiH​/LRi​∈(0,1]. The elasticity μU,g\mu_{U,g}μU,g​ is group specific: the estimates are μU,H=1.105\mu_{U,H}=1.105μU,H​=1.105 and μU,L=0.769\mu_{U,L}=0.769μU,L​=0.769 (the latter not statistically different from zero).

The functional form says that what makes a neighborhood attractive is who lives there and not how many live there, in contrast to density-based amenities in Ahlfeldt et al. (2015); the motivation is that in a city with weak public goods the rich pay for private security and other local services. As with productivity, the effect is external to individual location choices and is a source of inefficiency. It also generates segregation: an inflow of college residents raises amenities, which attracts more of them, more strongly so if μU,H>μU,L\mu_{U,H}>\mu_{U,L}μU,H​>μU,L​.

The first is the closed-city assumption: each group's population Lˉg\bar{L}_gLˉg​ is fixed and must equal the sum of its residents over all locations iii and car-ownership states aaa. Together with the residential supply equation (6) it pins down the constant λU,g\lambda_{U,g}λU,g​, and hence the welfare level Uˉg\bar{U}_gUˉg​ in equation (8): in a closed city a transit improvement shows up as a change in Uˉg\bar{U}_gUˉg​. The open-city alternative lets the city population respond to Uˉg\bar{U}_gUˉg​ with migration elasticity ρ\rhoρ, so that part of the gain is dissipated in higher rents.

The second condition defines the lump-sum rebate. Total land rents are residential rents rRiHRir_{Ri}H_{Ri}rRi​HRi​ plus commercial rents rFiHFir_{Fi}H_{Fi}rFi​HFi​ summed over locations; dividing by total population Lˉ=∑gLˉg\bar{L}=\sum_g\bar{L}_gLˉ=∑g​Lˉg​ gives an equal payment π\piπ per resident, regardless of group or location. This payment enters income additively in equations (1) and (6). Commercial rents are valued at the full price rFir_{Fi}rFi​ and not at the landowner's return (1−τi)rFi(1-\tau_i)r_{Fi}(1−τi​)rFi​, so the revenue from the land use wedge is also returned to residents.

Rebating rents keeps all income inside the city, so that changes in floorspace prices are transfers among residents and the first-order welfare effect in Proposition 2 is the VTTS alone; with absentee landlords higher rents would be a leakage. Because π\piπ is the same in levels for everybody, it is a larger share of income for the low-skilled. Extensions with local home ownership or with all residents renting change the distributional results only slightly.

This equation defines the class of models to which the sufficient-statistics result applies. A model belongs to the class if, for every location iii, its equilibrium can be written as KKK conditions indexed by hhh (a residential supply equation, a housing market clearing condition, a labor demand equation, and so on), each of which is a product of powers of the KKK endogenous variables ykiy_{ki}yki​ on the left and, on the right, a constant λh\lambda_hλh​ common to all locations, the two access terms with exponents bhRb^R_hbhR​ and bhFb^F_hbhF​, and a residual eihe_{ih}eih​ made of exogenous location fundamentals. The exponent αkh\alpha_{kh}αkh​ is the elasticity with which variable kkk enters condition hhh (unrelated to the labor share αs\alpha_sαs​). The essential restriction is that the commuting network appears only inside ΦRi\Phi_{Ri}ΦRi​ and ΦFi\Phi_{Fi}ΦFi​, which in turn requires a gravity equation for commuting so that the CMA system of equation (18) holds.

The change in RCMA varies only by origin, car ownership and group, and is absorbed by the fixed effect γiag\gamma_{iag}γiag​; the change in wages varies only by destination and group, and is absorbed by δjg\delta_{jg}δjg​. The coefficient on the change in travel time is the product θgκ\theta_g\kappaθg​κ; with κ=0.012\kappa=0.012κ=0.012 taken from the mode choice model, dividing gives θg\theta_gθg​. Identification comes from changes in travel times across destinations for the same origin cell, net of what is common to a destination, that is, from the differential improvement of particular origin-destination links. The identifying assumption is that these changes are uncorrelated with changes in unobserved pair-specific commute costs Δξija\Delta\xi_{ija}Δξija​; the preferred estimates instrument Δtija\Delta t_{ija}Δtija​ with the placement instruments and give θH=2.44\theta_H=2.44θH​=2.44 and θL=4\theta_L=4θL​=4. A lower θg\theta_gθg​ means more dispersed match productivities, so commuting responds less to time.

This is the falsification test based on the staggered opening of the three phases. The unit iii is a census tract. The dependent variable is the change in the log of an outcome yiy_iyi​ (population, employment, floorspace prices) between t−ℓt-\ellt−ℓ and ttt. The first regressor is the change in log CMA over the same window, caused by lines that opened during it; its coefficient βCurrent\beta^{Current}βCurrent is the reduced-form elasticity of equation (19). The second regressor is the change in log CMA between ttt and t+kt+kt+k, caused by lines that open only after the outcome window has closed. The vector XiX_iXi​ holds the baseline controls and εi\varepsilon_iεi​ is the error. Resident CMA is used for residential outcomes and firm CMA for commercial ones.

The logic is that of a pre-trend test. If routes were placed in tracts that were already growing faster for unobserved reasons, tracts that will receive access in the future should already show faster growth today, and βFuture\beta^{Future}βFuture would be positive. Under the identifying assumption that CMA growth is uncorrelated with unobserved trends in amenities and productivities, future CMA growth should not predict current outcomes:

H0: βFuture=0H_0:\ \beta^{Future}=0H0​: βFuture=0

The test also checks that βCurrent\beta^{Current}βCurrent is stable when the future term is added, since current and future CMA growth are correlated across tracts. A caveat is anticipation: forward-looking floorspace prices could respond before opening, which would make βFuture≠0\beta^{Future}\neq0βFuture=0 without invalidating the design. In the results future CMA is insignificant except for total census employment, where the coefficient is driven by outliers.

This is the event-study specification for annual residential floorspace prices around the opening of phase 3. The dependent variable is the log price rRitr_{Rit}rRit​ in tract iii and year ttt. Tract fixed effects αi\alpha_iαi​ absorb permanent differences in price levels, locality-year effects γℓ(i)t\gamma_{\ell(i)t}γℓ(i)t​ absorb shocks common to the locality ℓ(i)\ell(i)ℓ(i) containing the tract, and δt′Xi\delta_t'X_iδt′​Xi​ lets the baseline controls (plus the change in CMA from the first two phases) have a different effect in every year. The treatment is continuous and time invariant: Δ12,06ln⁡ΦRi\Delta_{12,06}\ln\Phi_{Ri}Δ12,06​lnΦRi​ is the change in log resident CMA caused by the lines that opened in phase 3.

As printed in the article and in the note, the sum does not show the event-time indicator. It should be read as

∑τ=−86βτ 1[t−t0=τ]Δ12,06ln⁡ΦRi\sum_{\tau=-8}^{6}\beta^{\tau}\,\mathbf{1}\left[t-t_0=\tau\right]\Delta_{12,06}\ln\Phi_{Ri}τ=−8∑6​βτ1[t−t0​=τ]Δ12,06​lnΦRi​

where t0t_0t0​ is the opening year of phase 3, so that for each tract-year exactly one term is active. Without the indicator the coefficients βτ\beta^{\tau}βτ could not be separately identified, and the whole term would be collinear with αi\alpha_iαi​. One period must be omitted as the reference, so each βτ\beta^{\tau}βτ measures the elasticity of prices to the phase 3 change in CMA at τ\tauτ years from opening relative to the reference year.

Coefficients for τ<0\tau<0τ<0 test for pre-trends: they should be flat if tracts with large future gains in access were not already on different price paths. Coefficients for τ≥0\tau\geq0τ≥0 trace out the dynamic response; they are comparable to the long-difference elasticity βrR\beta_{r_R}βrR​​ of equation (19). The estimates are flat before opening, rise by about 0.5 in the year before opening (anticipation) and by a further 0.75 by year six.

These are the moment conditions of the GMM estimator of {ηg,μU,g,μA}\{\eta_g,\mu_{U,g},\mu_A\}{ηg​,μU,g​,μA​}. Each states that a structural error is uncorrelated with a set of instruments built from the placement instruments (the 1921 tram network and the least-cost construction path), conditional on the fixed effects and controls.

The first line concerns the residual of equation (25), unobserved amenity growth Δln⁡ϵRiag\Delta\ln\epsilon_{Riag}ΔlnϵRiag​, which for given parameters is computed as

It is interacted with three instruments: predicted growth in net income, which shifts the common utility and identifies ηg\eta_gηg​, and the two instruments of equation (26), which shift the college share and identify μU,g\mu_{U,g}μU,g​. For each group there are three moments for two parameters, so the residential block is overidentified.

The second line concerns the residual of equation (27), unobserved productivity growth Δln⁡ϵFis=Δln⁡Ais−μAΔln⁡L~Fi−γℓ−γF′Controlsi\Delta\ln\epsilon_{Fis}=\Delta\ln A_{is}-\mu_A\Delta\ln\tilde{L}_{Fi}-\gamma_{\ell}-\gamma_F'\text{Controls}_iΔlnϵFis​=ΔlnAis​−μA​ΔlnL~Fi​−γℓ​−γF′​Controlsi​, interacted with predicted growth in firm CMA for low- and high-skilled workers. These act as labor supply shocks to a workplace and identify μA\mu_AμA​ (two moments, one parameter). In the notation, the instrument set is indexed by skill ggg while the residual is indexed by industry sss: both instruments are applied to every tract-industry residual.

The moments are stacked and estimated jointly. Because the observations differ across blocks (tract by group by car ownership on one side, tract by industry on the other), standard errors come from a block bootstrap that resamples tracts. Validity rests on the placement instruments being unrelated to changes in amenity and productivity fundamentals, the same assumption as in the reduced-form IV.
